title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
directAnswer: There's no BST ordering to exploit here, so you can't compare values — you must search. Do a single post-order DFS that returns a node if the subtree rooted there contains p or q (or is p/q itself). At each node, look at what the left and right subtrees reported: if BOTH came back non-null, the two targets are on opposite sides, so THIS node is the LCA. If only one side reported a target, bubble that result up. The first node where the two searches converge is the answer.

remember.pattern: Post-order DFS that bubbles up p/q sightings; split point is the LCA
remember.formula:
lca(node, p, q):
    if node is null or node == p or node == q: return node
    left  = lca(node.left,  p, q)
    right = lca(node.right, p, q)
    if left and right: return node      # p and q split here → LCA
    return left != null ? left : right  # both on one side (or none)
rules: This is a **plain** binary tree — no value ordering, so you must search both subtrees, not navigate by comparison.
Base case returns the node itself when it **equals p or q** — a node can be its own ancestor.
If **both** children return non-null, the current node is the **split point** → it's the LCA.
If only **one** side returns non-null, propagate that result upward — the LCA is higher or is that returned node.
Recurse **post-order**: gather left and right answers *before* deciding at the current node.
whenToUse: Find the lowest node that is an ancestor of two given nodes in an UNORDERED binary tree
Both p and q are guaranteed to exist in the tree
A node may be an ancestor of itself (p is an ancestor of q)
You want a single O(n) pass without parent pointers
antiSignals: Tree is a BST → compare values to walk down in O(h) (LCA of a BST)
Nodes have parent pointers → walk up and intersect the two ancestor chains
p or q might NOT exist → you must verify presence, changing the return contract
Many repeated queries on a static tree → preprocess with binary lifting / Euler tour + RMQ
remember.takeaway: LCA in a general binary tree is the canonical 'bubble-up a sighting' post-order: each node reports whether a target lives below it, and the unique node that hears 'yes' from both sides is where the paths to p and q diverge. Master this and you've mastered the post-order aggregation pattern.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realize that without BST ordering you must search both subtrees, and whether you express the answer as a post-order aggregation: the node where left and right searches both succeed is the LCA.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to compare p.val and q.val against node.val (only valid for a BST), or returning too early / mishandling the case where one target is an ancestor of the other (p inside q's subtree).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the post-order contract precisely — 'each call returns p, q, the LCA, or null' — and explain why returning the node itself in the base case correctly handles the ancestor-of-itself case without special-casing it.

problemStatement:
Given a binary tree, find the **lowest common ancestor (LCA)** of two given nodes `p` and `q` in the tree.

The lowest common ancestor is defined as the lowest node in the tree that has both `p` and `q` as descendants, where we allow **a node to be a descendant of itself** (so if `p` is an ancestor of `q`, the LCA of `p` and `q` is `p`).
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10⁵]
p ≠ q and both p and q exist in the tree
understanding: We need the deepest node that has both p and q somewhere in its subtree. 'Lowest' means closest to p and q (farthest from the root). Because the tree is not a BST, there's no shortcut by value comparison — we genuinely have to find where the downward paths to p and q split. The guarantee that both nodes exist lets us keep the return logic simple.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is this a binary search tree or a general binary tree?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: General. That's crucial — for a BST you'd compare values and descend in O(h); here you must search both subtrees.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are p and q guaranteed to be in the tree?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That lets the base case simply return a node on match without verifying both targets were actually found.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a node be an ancestor of itself?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — if p sits inside q's subtree, then q is the LCA. The base case 'return node if it equals p or q' handles this for free.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are there parent pointers available?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. With parent pointers you could walk up from p and q and intersect their ancestor chains; here we recurse from the root.

examples.explanation: 5 is in the left subtree of 3 and 1 is in the right subtree, so the paths split at the root 3.
4 is a descendant of 5 (5 → 2 → 4), so 5 is its own-and-q's ancestor — the LCA is 5.
2 is a child of 1; 1 is an ancestor of both itself and 2, so the LCA is 1.

approaches.name: Single Post-Order DFS (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it's the expected answer. Frame it as 'one bottom-up pass where each node reports whether p or q is below it'.
hints: There's no value ordering to exploit, so you can't decide which way to go by comparing — you must look in both subtrees. What should a recursive call tell its parent?
Make each call return: the node if it IS p or q, otherwise whatever its subtrees found. Think about what it means when both the left and right calls come back non-null.

If left and right both return something, p and q are on opposite sides, so the current node is their lowest common ancestor. If only one side returns a node, pass it up — the answer is at or above it.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single DFS visits each node once with O(1) work per node → O(n) time. Recursion depth equals the tree height h → O(h) stack space, O(log n) balanced and O(n) degenerate.
approaches.explanation:
Without a BST's ordering we cannot decide which direction p or q lies by comparing values, so the algorithm is fundamentally a *search* of both subtrees combined with a clever return contract. The contract is the heart of it: **each recursive call returns a node that 'represents' what was found in its subtree** — either `p`, `q`, the LCA itself if already determined, or `null` if neither target is present below.

**Why the base case returns the node on a match.** When we hit `null` we return `null` (nothing here). When we hit `p` or `q` we return that node — even without checking whether the *other* target is below it. This is the move that elegantly handles 'a node is an ancestor of itself'. Suppose `p` is an ancestor of `q`. The DFS reaches `p` and immediately returns `p`. Higher up, the side containing `p` reports `p`, the other side reports `null`, so we propagate `p` upward — and since `q` lives beneath `p`, no node above ever sees a second non-null sibling, so `p` correctly emerges as the answer.

**Why 'both sides non-null' identifies the LCA.** After recursing, examine `left` and `right`. If *both* are non-null, then one target was found somewhere in the left subtree and the other in the right subtree. The only node that has p in one subtree and q in the other is precisely the node where their root-to-node paths diverge — by definition the lowest common ancestor. So we return the current node, and because we're unwinding *post-order* (bottom-up), the *first* (lowest) such split point is the one that gets locked in; nodes above it will only ever see this single result on one side.

**Why one-sided results bubble up unchanged.** If only `left` is non-null, every target found so far lives in the left subtree, so the answer is at or above the node `left` points to — we return `left` untouched. Symmetrically for `right`. If both are null, neither target is below, so we return `null`. This propagation is what carries the eventual answer all the way up to the root without re-deriving it.

**Why post-order is mandatory.** We must know what *both* subtrees found before we can decide anything at the current node — a pre-order decision would be premature because we haven't searched below yet. Gathering `left` and `right` first, then deciding, is the textbook post-order shape, and it's why this whole family of problems (subtree aggregation, diameter, balanced check) shares the same skeleton.
approaches.insight: The single trick is overloading the return value: a non-null return means 'a target (or the LCA) lives in or below me'. The unique node that receives a non-null report from BOTH children is where p and q's paths split — and post-order guarantees we detect the lowest such node first. No parent pointers, no second pass, one O(n) sweep.

pitfalls: Comparing p.val/q.val with node.val as if it were a BST — invalid ordering in a general tree.
Forgetting that a node can be its own ancestor, then special-casing it incorrectly.
Stopping the search at the first target without searching the other subtree — breaks the both-sides test.
Using == on values instead of node identity when duplicate-looking nodes exist (values are unique here, but identity is the safe habit).

approaches.name: Parent-Pointer Mapping + Ancestor-Set Intersection
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as an alternative when asked for another method, or when parent pointers exist. Useful intuition: it mirrors the linked-list intersection trick.
hints: If you knew each node's parent, finding the LCA would be like finding where two paths to the root meet.
First DFS/BFS the tree recording each node's parent in a map. Then walk from p up to the root, storing every ancestor in a set.
Now walk from q upward; the first ancestor already in p's set is the lowest common ancestor.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the parent map visits every node once → O(n). Collecting p's ancestors is O(h), and walking q upward is O(h). Storage for the parent map and ancestor set is O(n).
approaches.explanation:
This approach reduces LCA to the classic 'intersection of two upward paths' problem by first manufacturing the parent links the tree doesn't natively provide. It's especially natural when the node type *does* carry a parent pointer.

**Step one: record parents.** A single traversal from the root builds a map `child → parent`. We stop early once both `p` and `q` have been assigned parents, since we only need the ancestor chains of those two nodes, but building the full map is also fine and keeps the code simple.

**Step two: collect p's ancestor chain.** Starting at `p`, repeatedly hop to the parent, inserting each node into a set, until we pass the root. This set is exactly the set of nodes on the path from `p` up to and including the root — every node that is an ancestor of `p` (counting `p` itself).

**Step three: walk q up until we hit that set.** Now climb from `q` toward the root. The *first* node we encounter that is already in `p`'s ancestor set is, by construction, an ancestor of both `p` and `q`. Because we climb from `q` and stop at the very first hit, it is also the *lowest* such common ancestor — any higher common ancestor would be encountered later. That first intersection is the LCA.

**Why this is essentially the linked-list-intersection trick.** Each node's chain of parents up to the root is a linked list, and two such lists share a common suffix (the path from the LCA to the root). Finding the LCA is finding the *start* of that shared suffix — identical in spirit to finding where two linked lists merge. The trade-off versus the single-DFS solution is explicit `O(n)` space for the parent map and ancestor set, in exchange for a more mechanical, two-phase structure that some find easier to reason about and that generalizes when parent pointers are already present.
approaches.insight: LCA equals the first meeting point of the two upward paths to the root. Once you see each node's ancestor chain as a linked list sharing a common tail, this becomes the same problem as intersection of two linked lists — a satisfying cross-pattern connection worth mentioning.

pitfalls: Forgetting to add p itself to its ancestor set, missing the ancestor-of-itself case.
Looping forever if the parent map is incomplete (didn't traverse far enough).
Using O(n) space when the single-DFS solution needs only O(h) — call out the trade-off.
Comparing by value instead of node identity when populating the maps.

commonMistakes: Treating the tree as a BST and comparing values to decide direction.
Not handling the case where one target is an ancestor of the other.
Returning early before searching both subtrees, breaking the both-sides split test.
Doing the decision pre-order instead of post-order, before subtree results are known.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using BST value comparison on a general tree
commonMistakesDetailed.why: LCA of a BST navigates by comparing values, but a general binary tree has no ordering. Comparing node.val to p.val/q.val sends you down the wrong branch.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Mishandling ancestor-of-itself
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you require BOTH subtrees to confirm a target before returning a node, you miss the case where q lives under p — p should win, but the over-strict check returns null.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Deciding pre-order before subtree results exist
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The both-sides test requires knowing what each subtree found. Returning the current node before recursing into both children produces wrong answers because you haven't located the targets yet.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if (root == p || root == q) return root;
if (lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q) != null) return root;  // premature: subtrees not both searched

patternNote: Post-order aggregation that bubbles a 'sighting' upward. Recognise it whenever the answer depends on information from both subtrees combined at the node above them. The same shape — recurse both sides, then decide — powers Diameter of Binary Tree, Balanced Binary Tree, and Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum.
